title: Jim Experiences Learning to Read as an Adult
author: Terry Underwood
summary: Terry Underwood revisits a decades-old interview with Jim, a janitor who is learning to read as an adult through a volunteer Laubach phonics tutor at the public library. Jim's account of his schooling shows how reading failure was manufactured: a punitive first-grade teacher, a bottom-row reading group, special-education shuffling, and rote spelling punishments that taught him to game the work rather than learn. Underwood reads this through the factory model of education, in which finite remediation resources were withdrawn from the children least likely to profit. The tutoring succeeds because it combines a human connection, explicit phonics, and a tutor who refuses to supply words and makes Jim do the work of turning print into speech. Underwood adds a Freirean note, that the learner begins to move from asking how to read to asking why he was not taught, and closes with the history of the 1977 functional-literacy statistic and an open question about adult literacy today. The piece is a case study rather than a research argument, but it makes the cost of poor early reading instruction concrete.
points: Jim's schooling shows how ability grouping and special-education tracking can stop a child's reading development while appearing to serve him.
Rote punishment spelling (write it 25, 50, then 100 times) produced shortcuts and disengagement rather than learning to spell.
Jim's adult progress came from a tutor who built a human connection first, then used explicit phonics and made him decode words himself.
Underwood frames the story with the factory model of education, where remediation is rationed by efficiency and the least promising students are dropped.
The 1977 functional-illiteracy figure and its dismissal show how adult literacy gets defined and contested, and the definition keeps getting harder to meet.
quotes: Unfortunately, Jim enjoyed none of the advantages but all of the disadvantages of ability grouping in reading. He carried indelibly in his metaphors his feelings about being in the bad reading group.

Within a few weeks Jim had picked up some phonics skills. He discovered residual learning stuck somewhere in his brain, surprising himself with how much he could do with help. He was excited about his progress.
Let’s make it ‘the.’ So I would write tttt, you know, 75 times or a hunnert times, hhhh it didn’t matter to me because I figured I wasn’t going to learn to spell that way. Big deal, writin’ it down.

Jim remembered being left out in the cold in high school. The logic of the factory metaphor—the famous factory model of education—must have forced the urban school district to allocate finite resources according to principle of efficiency. As children got older, those with the least—or no—chance of profiting from reading instruction were removed from remediation to make room for those with a better chance.

Jim credited his tutor’s consistent focus on monitoring him and making him do the work of turning print into speech as key to his development. If I had been more on the ball forty years ago, I would have asked to observe a tutoring session. He also praised the Laubach materials.

I had been reading and rereading Freire’s Pedagogy of the Oppressed for about a year at the time, keeping a reflective journal, and noted that Jim was on the cusp of a milestone: When the oppressed pivot from asking “How do I read?” to asking, “Why was I not taught to read?” the pedagogy is taking.

The core finding had staying power. Whether you agree with the conceptual framework of the APL regarding what behaviors count as evidence of “functional illiteracy,” the published finding that “21.7% of American adults are functionally illiterate” became the default position.
